chunks: UART oversampling and common rates. The question: What is oversampling? How is it implemented? Why is it needed? What are some common oversample rates for UART?
Oversampling means the UART receiver looks at the incoming line many times during each bit, not just once. The usual choice is 16 looks per bit.
The receiver counts these looks, called ticks, to find the middle of each bit. It also uses several looks near the middle to outvote a brief noise spike.
The cost is that the receiver's counting clock must run 16 times faster than the baud rate, the number of bits per second.
Imagine watching a traffic light by glancing at it. If you glance only once per light cycle, you cannot tell when it changed.
If you glance 16 times per cycle, you can say roughly when it flipped, within one glance. Count 8 glances after the flip and you are at the middle of the phase.
Take three glances around that point and go with the majority.
The receive-side flow. The tick counter is the whole mechanism: count to N over 2 for the centre of the start bit, then count N for each bit.
In real chips this is a small counter plus a shift register.
Oversampling factor: how many ticks the receiver counts per bit. 16 is the classic. 8 is common on modern chips.
Tick: one step of the receiver's fast counting clock, 1/16 of a bit at 16x.
Majority vote: taking three samples near the bit's middle and using the value that at least two agree on.
At 115200 baud with 16x oversampling, a tick is about 0. 54 microseconds. The receiver sees the line fall and starts counting. After 8 ticks, about 4.
3 microseconds, it checks the line is still low. Then it looks every 16 ticks, about 8. 7 microseconds, so each look lands near the middle of a bit.
It may use ticks 7, 8 and 9 and take the majority.
With a 48 megahertz clock, 16x allows at most 3 Mbaud, and 8x allows 6 Mbaud, since the maximum is the clock divided by the factor. That is the whole idea.
"Oversampling means the receiver samples the line at a multiple of the baud rate, typically 16x. A counter runs at 16 times the baud.
When it sees the falling start edge it counts 8 ticks to reach the middle of the start bit, confirms it's low, then samples every 16 ticks, so each sample lands mid-bit.
It often takes three samples around the centre and majority-votes.
It's needed because there's no clock: finding the bit centre and rejecting noise needs finer resolution than one sample per bit.
16x is classic; 8x is common on modern MCUs to reach higher baud rates."
